title: What Public Health Initiatives Looked Like in the Middle Ages - Nautilus
gist: A new multidisciplinary book challenges the view that medieval Europe lacked public health efforts, examining how Trondheim's residents responded to disease as the city grew from ~250 to ~3,000 people and scholars brought miasma theory.

insights.claim: A new book challenges the assumption that medieval Europe made no major public-health advances, using a multidisciplinary approach to show how Trondheim's citizens grappled with illness.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Trondheim's population grew from roughly 250 around 950 CE to 1,500 by the 12th century, then doubled to about 3,000 during the High Middle Ages.
insights.so_what: Urban density growth as a driver of public-health responses.
insights.locator: Trondheim’s population exploded in the Early
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Monks, scholars and the archbishop arriving in Trondheim brought new theories of disease, notably miasma theory, the idea that illness spread by foul odors.
insights.so_what: Shows how imported expertise shaped municipal health policy.
